title: The neat streets of the Indus Valley
description: Four and a half thousand years ago, the cities of the Indus Valley had grid streets, covered drains and indoor bathrooms — then quietly faded from memory for millennia.

body.heading: Cities planned from the start
paragraphs: Around 2600 BC, in what is now Pakistan and north-west India, the people of the Indus Valley built cities that look planned rather than grown. Mohenjo-daro, the best known, laid its streets in a grid, built with baked bricks of standard sizes used across the whole civilisation.

Most remarkably, the houses connected to covered drains that carried wastewater away — a level of civic plumbing that many later cities would not match for thousands of years. Many homes had their own wells and bathing rooms.

body.heading: A civilisation without obvious kings
paragraphs: Archaeologists have found no great palaces, royal tombs or towering monuments to rulers in Indus cities. There is a large, carefully built bath at Mohenjo-daro, granaries and workshops — but power, if it existed, left few boasts behind.

The Indus people traded widely, sending beads, cotton and timber as far as Mesopotamia, whose texts mention a rich land called Meluhha. Their craftspeople produced exquisite tiny seals, carved with animals and signs.

body.heading: The script that will not speak
paragraphs: Those signs are the civilisation's great unsolved puzzle. The Indus script survives only in short inscriptions, mostly a handful of characters long, with no bilingual text to unlock it. Despite a century of attempts and many claimed solutions, it remains undeciphered.

Around 1900 BC the cities emptied, likely as rivers shifted and trade faltered, and the civilisation was forgotten until excavations in the 1920s revealed it again — a reminder that even the best-plumbed cities depend on water, and that history can misplace a whole civilisation for four thousand years.

takeaway: Indus cities pioneered urban planning and drains, left no obvious kings, and kept one secret: a script nobody has yet learned to read.
